glosses: To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite.

examples.text: There’s no need to rehearse the same old argument; we’ve heard it before, and we all agree.

glosses: To narrate; to relate; to tell; to recount.

examples.text: The witness rehearsed the events of the night before for the listening detectives.

glosses: To practise by recitation or repetition in private for experiment and improvement, prior to a public representation, especially in theater.

examples.text: I ſuppoſe vve ſhall hardly Rehearſe the Comedy this Morning; for the Author vvas Arreſted as he vvas going home from King's Coffee-houſe; and, as I heard, it vvas for upvvards of Four Pound: I ſuppoſe he vvill hardly get Bail.
The main actors spent on average two hours a day rehearsing before the first night.

In sober mornings, do not thou reherse / The holy incantation of a verse ...

glosses: To cause to rehearse; to instruct by rehearsal.

examples.text: The director rehearsed the cast incessantly in the days leading up to opening night, and as a result they were tired and cranky when it arrived.
He […] has been rehearsed by Madame Defarge as to his having seen Her […]
It was plain that he'd been rehearsed a lot, but he wasn't letter-perfect by any manner of means.

glosses: To contrive and carefully prepare (a story, etc.) to offer consistency.

examples.text: The Crown argued that the accused had rehearsed her story.
